grammar.name: Passive voice in present and past
grammar.explanation: Use the passive when the action matters more than the doer, or when the doer is obvious, unknown or already understood.
keyPoints: Present passive: The old town is visited by two million people a year.
Past passive: The temple was built in the eleventh century.
Keep the agent with by only when it adds information.
grammar.example: The festival is celebrated every spring, and the square was decorated by local families for generations.

items.prompt: The temple ___ in the eleventh century.
items.explanation: A finished past action with an unknown or unimportant agent takes the past passive.

items.prompt: Choose the best sentence for a travel guide.
options: Two million people visit the old town every year.
The old town is visited by two million people every year.
The old town visits two million people every year.
items.answer: The old town is visited by two million people every year.
items.explanation: Guides foreground the place, so the passive keeps the old town as the topic.

options: When the agent is unknown, obvious or unimportant
items.answer: When the agent is unknown, obvious or unimportant
items.explanation: The agent is optional; include it only if it carries new information.

grammar.name: Relative clauses: defining and non-defining
grammar.explanation: Defining clauses identify which person or place you mean and take no commas; non-defining clauses add extra information and always take commas.
keyPoints: Defining: The village that we visited is now a tourist trap.
Non-defining: Lisbon, which I visited last year, is crowded in August.
Never use that in a non-defining clause, and never drop the relative pronoun after a comma.
grammar.example: The guide, who grew up in the old quarter, showed us a market that no tourist ever finds.

items.prompt: Lisbon, ___ I visited last year, is crowded in August.
items.explanation: Non-defining clauses about a thing take which, never that.

options: The guide who grew up here knows every street.
My brother who lives in Berlin is visiting.
items.explanation: Commas change meaning: with them the clause is extra information; without them it identifies the person.

items.prompt: The town ___ we stayed had no tourists at all.
items.explanation: Where replaces a place adverbial: we stayed in the town.

inputs.title: Travel podcast: the case for slow travel
inputs.body: People often ask me how many countries I have been to, and I have started saying that I have no idea, because the number tells you nothing. I spent three weeks in one town in Portugal last spring. I learned the baker's name. I was invited to a birthday party. That would never have happened if I had been moving every two days. Slow travel is not about seeing less; it is about being seen, and remembered, as a guest rather than a customer.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker reject the country count?
options: It says nothing about the experience
It is too difficult to count
questions.answer: It says nothing about the experience

questions.prompt: What did she do last spring?
options: Stayed three weeks in one town
questions.answer: Stayed three weeks in one town

inputs.title: When tourism becomes too much
inputs.body: Venice is not alone. From Barcelona to Kyoto, cities that were built for residents are now shaped by visitors. Short-let flats have pushed rents up, and the bakery that survived for sixty years has been replaced by a shop selling souvenirs made elsewhere. Some cities have responded with visitor taxes, caps on cruise ships or bans on new short-term lets. None of these measures is popular with everyone. Yet the question behind them is simple: is a city a place to live, or a place to be seen? Most residents would answer both, and they would add that the balance has tipped.

questions.prompt: What is the article mainly about?
options: The effects of mass tourism on cities
The best time to visit Venice
questions.answer: The effects of mass tourism on cities

writing.title: Descriptive article: a place worth protecting
writing.prompt: Write a 160–180-word descriptive article about a place you know that is changing because of tourism. Describe it, explain what is changing, and suggest one measure.

outline.analyze: Purpose: inform and persuade. Audience: curious travellers. Register: semi-formal.
outline.plan: Vivid opening → what makes the place special → the pressure → one suggestion → closing line.
outline.draft: Use at least three passives and one non-defining relative clause.
outline.improve: Replace general adjectives with concrete details; add a concession.
outline.review: Check that every passive has a clear reason for being passive.

grammar.name: Modals of deduction: must, might, could, can't
grammar.explanation: Use must when you are almost certain, might or could when something is possible, and can't when you are almost certain it is untrue.
keyPoints: Certain: The update must have broken the app.
Possible: She might be working from home.
Impossible: That can't be the reason they cancelled.
grammar.example: The site is down, so they must be updating the servers; it could also be a network problem.

items.prompt: The site is down. They ___ be updating the servers.
items.explanation: Must expresses strong certainty based on evidence.

items.prompt: That ___ be the reason — the app works fine on other phones.
items.explanation: Can't marks a conclusion you are almost certain is wrong.

items.prompt: Which sentence leaves the possibility open?

grammar.name: Reported speech and reporting verbs
grammar.explanation: When you report speech, shift the tense back one step and adjust pronouns and time expressions; reporting verbs such as claim, admit and warn change the pattern that follows.
keyPoints: 'I will fix it tomorrow.' → She said she would fix it the next day.
Reporting verb + -ing: He admitted breaking the rules.
Reporting verb + to: They warned us not to share the link.
grammar.example: The engineer said the update would take two days, admitted that the testing had been rushed, and warned us not to reinstall.

items.prompt: 'I will fix it tomorrow.' → She said she ___ it the next day.
items.explanation: Will shifts to would in reported speech.

inputs.title: Tech news: the week in AI
inputs.body: A major video platform has announced that AI-generated clips must now be labelled. The company said the change would take effect within thirty days and admitted that earlier labelling had been inconsistent. Researchers welcomed the move but warned that labels alone will not stop misinformation, because most people share a clip before they read the caption. One campaign group claimed the policy was 'too little, too late', while the platform insisted that it was a first step.

options: Labels are not enough on their own
questions.answer: Labels are not enough on their own

inputs.title: The price of a free app
inputs.body: Nothing on your phone is free. When an app costs nothing to install, the cost is usually paid in attention or data. A typical free app requests access to location, contacts and microphone, and many users accept without reading the prompt. Regulators have begun to push back: several countries now require plain-language summaries of what an app collects. Yet the strongest protection remains unglamorous. Turn off permissions you do not use. Read the prompt. And remember that a service designed to keep you scrolling is not designed to help you leave.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main claim?
options: Free apps are paid for with attention or data
questions.answer: Free apps are paid for with attention or data

questions.prompt: What protection does the writer call strongest?

writing.title: Review: an app, film or product
writing.prompt: Write a 180-word review of an app, film or product for a general audience. Describe it, weigh its strengths and weaknesses, and give a clear recommendation.

outline.analyze: Purpose: evaluate and recommend. Audience: potential users or viewers. Register: semi-formal.
outline.plan: Hook → description → two strengths → one weakness → recommendation.
outline.draft: Use one modal of deduction and two reported-speech structures.
outline.improve: Replace vague praise with evidence; vary sentence length.
outline.review: Check that the recommendation matches the evidence you gave.
